nodes.name: Sago palm
nodes.desc: A palm of lowland swamp forests in New Guinea. Its trunk starch is a staple food for people along rivers such as the Sepik, and each stem flowers once and then dies while suckers carry on.

nodes.name: Fig trees
nodes.desc: Tropical forest figs fruit heavily and feed many birds and mammals, which spread the seeds. Each fig species relies on its own specialised wasp for pollination.

nodes.name: Schefflera
nodes.desc: Montane forest trees and shrubs whose fruit is a main food of the splendid astrapia.

nodes.name: Karuka pandanus
nodes.desc: A screwpine of montane forest between about 1,300 and 3,300 m. Its nuts are eaten by possums and several rodents, including Rothschild's woolly rat, as well as by people.

nodes.name: Southern beech
nodes.desc: New Guinea beeches characterise lower and upper montane rain forest. UNESCO notes the park's beech forests are well represented and are hit by Phytophthora dieback.

nodes.name: Subalpine shrubs
nodes.desc: Rhododendrons, heaths and other shrubs form the mossy shrubland and forest edge below the alpine zone.

nodes.name: Southern cassowary
nodes.desc: Forages on the forest floor for fallen fruit and seeds, including palms, and also takes fungi, insects, snails, small animals and carrion. Listed as threatened in the park.

nodes.name: Polynesian rat
nodes.desc: A small, widespread rodent that eats seeds, fruit and insects. It is among the most recorded mammals near the site.

nodes.name: Brown dorcopsis
nodes.desc: A forest wallaby of lowland and hill rainforest that feeds on plant matter on the forest floor. Forest wallabies are a main prey of the Papuan eagle.

nodes.name: Rothschild's woolly rat
nodes.desc: A giant rodent of New Guinea forests that eats karuka nuts. It is one of the larger rats recorded in the park.

nodes.name: Dingiso
nodes.desc: A tree-kangaroo of subalpine forest and shrubland at about 3,250 to 4,200 m, mostly living on the ground. Endangered, mainly because of hunting and habitat loss.

nodes.name: Splendid astrapia
nodes.desc: A bird-of-paradise of montane forest that eats mostly fruit, especially Schefflera and Pandanus, plus insects and small lizards and frogs.

nodes.name: Earthworms
nodes.desc: Soil animals that eat leaf litter and mix it into the soil. They are the food of the long-beaked echidna.

nodes.name: Long-beaked echidna
nodes.desc: An egg-laying mammal of hill and montane forest that feeds mainly on earthworms, unlike the ant-eating short-beaked echidna.

nodes.name: New Guinea quoll
nodes.desc: A climbing marsupial hunter of forests up to about 3,300 m. It takes birds, rats, other marsupials, reptiles and insects, and also scavenges.

nodes.name: Crocodile monitor
nodes.desc: A very long arboreal lizard of lowland rainforest and mangrove swamps. It eats birds, eggs, rats, bandicoots, frogs and carrion.

nodes.name: Papuan eagle
nodes.desc: A big forest eagle that hunts from the canopy. It takes possums, tree-kangaroos, forest wallabies and woolly rats, as well as birds and reptiles.

nodes.name: Highland wild dog
nodes.desc: Wild dogs live near the base of Puncak Jaya at roughly 3,900 to 4,200 m. New Guinea wild dogs eat marsupials, rodents, birds and fruit, and are said to steal eagle kills.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Equatorial sun reaches the lowlands year-round; cloud and altitude cut it back in the mountain forests.

nodes.name: Heavy rain
nodes.desc: Wet tropical climate across the park, from the Arafura coast to the summits.

nodes.name: Equatorial glaciers
nodes.desc: Five small glaciers on the highest peaks feed rivers down to the lowland swamps. UNESCO notes they are retreating quickly.

nodes.name: Forest soil
nodes.desc: The soil layer that supports lowland swamp, montane forest and shrubland.

nodes.name: Fungi & soil microbes
nodes.desc: Break down fallen leaves, wood and dead animals in the humid forest and return nutrients to the soil.
